feed.title: Quench blog
feed.subtitle: Building a JavaScript, TypeScript and WebAssembly engine in Rust

entry.title: Hello world in 4,896 bytes: AOT as the JIT run at build time
entry.summary: Quench now compiles a JavaScript hello world to a 4,896-byte native executable that starts in 0.96 ms with 1.3 MB of memory, level with C. No second compiler: the build runs the program through the same specializer as the JIT and keeps only what is left.

entry.title: Strict AOT: a compiler that refuses, and names the input
entry.summary: Running a program at build time is only safe if the build never bakes in something a later run would see differently. Quench's strict AOT mode is sound by construction: host operations off an allow-list are refused before they run, and the build names the input it could not fold.

entry.title: Chasing a sub-megabyte readline binary
entry.summary: A small TypeScript compiler turns a readline REPL into a binary under 1 MB that starts in about 1 ms. Quench's is 71 MB and starts in 6.2 ms. Where the megabytes go, what we have cut so far, and the general plan to close the gap without a single readline-specific path.

entry.title: From 538 to 224 seconds: rebuilding a JavaScript engine faster
entry.summary: A one-line change in the arithmetic of Quench's interpreter took 538 seconds to rebuild. Two days of profiling LLVM, sharding generated code and refusing any change that cost a single instruction at run time brought it to 224 seconds. What worked and what we rejected.

entry.title: Where Quench stands: JetStream 3 with the JIT off
entry.summary: Against Node and Bun with all JITs disabled, Quench sits between them on speed and well below both on memory. The full picture, including the tests where its memory is far too high.

entry.title: 3 × C + 6: an instruction budget for every JavaScript operation
entry.summary: Every primitive operation in Quench's interpreter now has a ceiling on the machine instructions it may execute, derived from the same operation written in C and enforced by a gate that only lets the number go down.

entry.title: The JIT compiled the code and then never ran it
entry.summary: On 33 of 44 primitive operations our optimizing JIT was no faster than the interpreter. For many of them the reason was simple and embarrassing: the native code existed and nothing ever jumped to it.

entry.title: Entry cells, exit descriptors and a collector without stack maps
entry.summary: Three small contracts decide how compiled JavaScript is called, how it gives up, and how the garbage collector finds its roots. Quench's versions are unusual, and this is the reasoning behind each.

entry.title: JavaScript that looks like C should cost what C costs
entry.summary: We wrote eight small kernels twice, once in JavaScript and once in C, and counted. The results set the standard Quench's compiled code is now held to, and showed one benchmark that had never been compiled at all.

entry.title: One interpreter, four outputs: Futamura projections in a JavaScript engine
entry.summary: Quench writes the meaning of each JavaScript operation once and derives the interpreter, a copy-and-patch JIT, an optimizing JIT and an AOT compiler from it. How that works, and an honest count of how far the code is from the design.

entry.title: A 17.6% regression that was four deleted globals
entry.summary: Thirty hours of running JetStream 3 every ninety minutes took the interpreter from 0.61 to 0.90 of the best competing engine, then lost a sixth of it overnight. The bisect led somewhere unexpected.

entry.title: AOT without a second compiler
entry.summary: We built a closed-world JavaScript-to-native compiler, measured it, and threw it away. Quench's ahead-of-time mode is the interpreter specialized to what is known at build time, and this is why.

entry.title: Most optimizations do not survive measurement
entry.summary: Notes from a ledger of rejected changes. Superinstructions, inline allocation, tail-call conventions and a 33% win on one benchmark, all turned down, and the rule that turned them down.

entry.title: Interpreter against interpreter: eight for eight, and the JIT that was not ready
entry.summary: With every engine's JIT turned off, Quench's interpreter led all eight classic V8 benchmarks. The same week its JIT trailed Node and Bun by 2 to 24 times. Both results are worth showing.

entry.title: Your peak RSS depends on which CPU you ran on
entry.summary: The same binary reported peak memory anywhere from 2,436 to 2,824 KiB across 20 runs. Four things we learned about measuring a JavaScript engine's memory before we could trust a single number.

entry.title: One 64-bit word, two narrow slots and three loads per field
entry.summary: How Quench represents values and objects, why an object reference is an index and not a pointer, and what that choice costs every time you read a field.

entry.title: The day we deleted 405,013 lines
entry.summary: Quench's second runtime replaced the first in a single commit that removed 405,013 lines. This is how the rewrite was staged so that the cutover was boring.

entry.title: We deleted our benchmark-specific fast paths
entry.summary: Our Richards score was good because the engine recognised the workload. We removed every path like that, took the lower numbers, and wrote the rule into the repository.

entry.title: 35,000 commits in a month
entry.summary: In August 2026 the repository took 35,083 commits, 4,217 of them in one day. Here is what that much parallel work built, what it broke, and what we changed so it could keep going.

entry.title: 4,367 class tests in two days, and what a skip list hides
entry.summary: Driving one test262 directory from 44 passing tests to all 4,367 taught us more about denominators than about classes.

entry.title: Quench started as a TypeScript-to-Rust transpiler
entry.summary: The first commit was a compiler driver, not a JavaScript engine. Four names, one embedded engine and one deleted interpreter later, the project admitted what it was becoming.
